title: Traffic signal concepts
source: Written from the ELECT 280 study guide; code values checked against the CA MUTCD 2026 and NEC where cited.

cards.front: In NEMA 8-phase numbering, what do odd and even phase numbers mean?
cards.back: Even phases (2, 4, 6, 8) are through movements. Odd phases (1, 3, 5, 7) are protected left turns.

cards.front: Which phases are usually the main street, and which the side street?
cards.back: Ø2 and Ø6 are the main-street throughs (opposite directions). Ø4 and Ø8 are the side-street throughs.

cards.front: Which through phase shares an approach with each left-turn phase?
cards.back: Ø1 with Ø6, Ø5 with Ø2, Ø3 with Ø8, Ø7 with Ø4. A left turn and the through on the same approach can run together.

cards.front: Which through phase does each left turn cross?
cards.back: Ø1 crosses Ø2, Ø5 crosses Ø6, Ø3 crosses Ø4, Ø7 crosses Ø8 (the opposing through).

cards.front: How do you decide which phase a signal head belongs to?
cards.back: By the traffic it faces, not the corner it stands on. Heads sit on the far side and face approaching drivers.
cards.note: A far-side head on the NE corner faces south and serves northbound traffic.

cards.front: Where do signal heads normally go, and how many does a through movement need?
cards.back: On the far side of the intersection. The CA MUTCD requires at least two primary signal faces for the through movement on an approach.

cards.front: What is the first thing to check on a signal plan before marking phases?
cards.back: The north arrow. Prints are often rotated so north is not up.

cards.front: Where is the final word on which direction is Ø2?
cards.back: The plan's phase diagram. Ø2 is often the main-street direction going north or east, but agencies differ.

cards.front: What is split phasing?
cards.back: The two directions of a street time one after the other (for example Ø3 then Ø4) instead of together, usually because of shared or heavy left turns.

cards.front: What is an overlap?
cards.back: An output tied to two or more phases, such as a right-turn arrow that is green during its parallel through and a compatible left turn. Overlaps A and B use 210 channels 9 and 10.

cards.front: What does a flashing yellow arrow (FYA) left-turn display mean?
cards.back: Permissive left turn: drivers may turn after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.

cards.front: Write out the standard dual-ring diagram.
cards.back: Ring 1: Ø1 Ø2 | Ø3 Ø4. Ring 2: Ø5 Ø6 | Ø7 Ø8. The barrier (|) separates the main-street group from the side-street group.

cards.front: What is concurrency?
cards.back: Two phases timing at the same time: one from Ring 1 and one from Ring 2, on the same side of the barrier.

cards.front: List the compatible phase pairs on each side of the barrier.
Can two phases in the same ring time together?
cards.back: No. Phases in one ring always conflict and time one after another.

cards.front: What is the barrier, and what rule applies to it?
cards.back: The line between main-street and side-street phases. Both rings must reach it and cross it together, because every main-street movement conflicts with every side-street movement.

cards.front: What three intervals make up a vehicle phase?
cards.back: Green, yellow change, and red clearance.

cards.front: What is the red clearance (all-red) interval?
cards.back: A time when every approach shows red, so a vehicle that entered on yellow can clear the intersection.

cards.front: Within what range should a yellow change interval fall?
cards.back: 3 to 6 seconds (CA MUTCD 4F.17). Longer yellows go with higher approach speeds.

cards.front: What is the kinematic formula for the yellow change interval?
cards.back: Y = t + v / (2a + 2gG), with t = 1 s, v in ft/s, a = 10 ft/s², g = 32.2 ft/s², G = grade as a decimal.
cards.note: 35 mph = 51.5 ft/s on a flat road gives about 3.6 s.

cards.front: CA MUTCD Table 4D-101(CA): which speed sets the minimum yellow?
cards.back: The 85th-percentile speed rounded up to the next 5 mph. If only the posted speed is known, add 7 mph (posted 30 mph or more) or 10 mph (25 mph or less).

cards.front: How long are red clearance intervals normally?
cards.back: 0.1 to 2.0 seconds, and they should not exceed 6 seconds except for unusual cases (CA MUTCD 4F.17).

cards.front: What is a lagging left turn?
cards.back: A left-turn phase that times after the opposing through, for example Ø5 after Ø2.

cards.front: What do the Caltrans Standard Plans sheets ES-1A to ES-1C cover?
cards.back: Electrical symbols, abbreviations, and how conduit runs are numbered.

cards.front: What comes first when the project plan and the Standard Plans disagree?
cards.back: The project documents: special provisions, then the project plans, then the Standard Plans, then the Standard Specifications.

cards.front: How do existing and new equipment look different on a plan?
cards.back: Existing equipment is drawn outlined or lighter; new equipment is drawn solid.

cards.front: Which two schedules on a signal plan list the equipment and wiring?
cards.back: The Standard and Equipment Schedule (poles, heads, push buttons, luminaires) and the Conduit and Conductor Schedule.

cards.front: What must you do before digging foundations or trenching conduit in California?
cards.back: Call 811 (USA North or DigAlert) at least two working days ahead so underground utilities are marked.

cards.front: Why read every note on a signal plan sheet?
cards.back: Notes can override the general rules, for example 'repull existing SIC only' in a run, and many say 'this sheet only'.

cards.front: Which vehicle phase does a ped phase run with?
cards.back: The parallel through phase: Ø2P with Ø2, Ø4P with Ø4, Ø6P with Ø6, Ø8P with Ø8.

cards.front: What are the pedestrian intervals, in order?
cards.back: Walk, flashing Don't Walk (pedestrian change interval), then steady Don't Walk.

cards.front: What walking speed sets the pedestrian clearance time?
cards.back: 3.5 ft/s (CA MUTCD 4I.06). Consider 2.8 ft/s where older or disabled pedestrians routinely cross.

cards.front: What second check must walk plus clearance pass?
cards.back: Walk + clearance must let someone leaving the push button (or 6 ft behind the curb) at the start of Walk cross at 3 ft/s.

cards.front: How long should the Walk interval be?
cards.back: At least 7 seconds; as short as 4 seconds is allowed where pedestrian volumes and needs don't require 7.

cards.front: What is the buffer interval added in the 2023 MUTCD?
cards.back: At least 2 seconds of steady Don't Walk after the flashing Don't Walk, before conflicting traffic is released.

cards.front: When is a countdown display required on a ped head?
cards.back: When the pedestrian change interval is more than 7 seconds (CA MUTCD 4I.04).

cards.front: How high are ped signal heads mounted?
cards.back: Bottom of the housing 7 to 10 feet above the sidewalk (CA MUTCD 4I.03).

cards.front: Where should a pedestrian push button be placed?
cards.back: No more than 5 ft from the outside edge of the crosswalk, 1.5 to 6 ft from the curb face, about 3.5 ft high (4 ft max), with its face parallel to the crosswalk.

cards.front: How far apart should two push buttons on one corner be?
cards.back: At least 10 feet. Closer than that, accessible signals must use speech walk messages.

cards.front: Does the push button on a pole always serve the ped head on that same pole?
cards.back: No. The button usually serves a different crosswalk from the head mounted on the same pole.

cards.front: What is a Leading Pedestrian Interval (LPI)?
cards.back: Walk starts a few seconds before the parallel green, so pedestrians get into the crosswalk before turning cars move.

cards.front: What is ped recall?
cards.back: The controller serves the ped phase every cycle without anyone pressing the button.

cards.front: How does an inductive loop detect a vehicle?
cards.back: The vehicle's metal carries eddy currents that lower the loop's inductance. The detector card sees its oscillator frequency rise and places a call.

cards.front: Does a vehicle over a loop raise or lower the loop's inductance?
cards.back: Lower.

cards.front: What does a vehicle detector designation like 2I2U mean?
cards.back: Phase 2, Input File I, slot 2, Upper channel.

cards.front: In a designation, what do U and L stand for?
cards.back: The upper and lower channel of the two-channel detector card. They do not mean upstream or limit line.

cards.front: Which input file holds which phases?
cards.back: Input File I holds Ø1–Ø4 detectors; Input File J holds Ø5–Ø8.

cards.front: Trace a loop's path from the street to the controller.
cards.back: Loop wire → splice in the pull box → DLC (detector lead-in cable) → input panel terminal block → input file slot → 222 detector card → controller.

cards.front: How many DLCs does each detector designation need?
cards.back: One DLC per designation, even when loops share a pull box.

cards.front: What inductance range do loop detector cards typically work with?
cards.back: About 50 to 700 µH (FHWA Traffic Detector Handbook).

cards.front: Why can't you measure a loop's impedance with an ohmmeter?
cards.back: An ohmmeter uses DC and reads only resistance. Impedance needs an AC measurement or an LCR meter.

cards.front: What must you do before meggering a loop?
cards.back: Unplug the 222 card and lift the lead-in. The megger's 500 or 1000 V test voltage will damage the card.

cards.front: How is the DLC shield grounded?
cards.back: At the cabinet end only, to reject noise without creating a ground loop.

cards.front: What does a long lead-in do to loop sensitivity?
cards.back: It adds inductance and resistance, so the vehicle's change is a smaller fraction of the total and sensitivity drops.

cards.front: List the 332L cage from top to bottom.
cards.back: 2070 controller, drawer shelf, Input File I, Input File J, PDA #2L (with the 206L power supply), Output File #1L.

cards.front: What does the 2070 controller do?
cards.back: Runs the timing program, reads detector and push-button calls, and drives the load switches with 24 VDC logic.

cards.front: What plugs into the input files?
cards.back: 222 two-channel loop detectors, 242 DC isolators (push buttons, flash sense), and other detector or isolator cards.

cards.front: What does the 242 in slot I14 provide?
cards.back: Flash Sense and Stop Time inputs to the controller.

cards.front: What is in the PDA #2L?
cards.back: Signal circuit breakers, two 204 flashers, the SSR, HI and K24 relays, and the 206L 24 VDC power supply.

cards.front: What is in Output File #1L?
cards.back: 12 Model 200 switch packs, 4 flash transfer relays (FTRs), the 210 monitor, and the flash program blocks on the back.

cards.front: What switches are on the police panel?
cards.back: Signals ON/OFF and AUTO/FLASH.

cards.front: Does Signals OFF make the cabinet safe to work in?
cards.back: No. It only removes power from the heads. The PDA, service panel and the controller's clean AC stay live.

cards.front: What happens if the 210 monitor is removed and the door is closed?
cards.back: The cabinet goes into flash. This is by design.

cards.front: How are the DC logic ground and AC wiring kept apart in a 332?
cards.back: The DC ground (white with a red stripe) runs separately from the AC wiring; AC neutral and equipment ground bond only at the service.

cards.front: What changes in the service panel when a battery backup system (BBS) is installed?
cards.back: The #8 jumper on the TBS terminal block is removed, and the BBS can keep the cabinet live during a utility outage.

cards.front: What does a Model 200 switch pack do?
cards.back: Three triac outputs switch 120 VAC to the field wires (R/Y/G or Don't Walk/Yellow/Walk) when the controller pulls the 24 VDC inputs low.

cards.front: How many switch packs does each PDA signal breaker feed?
cards.back: Three: a left turn, a through, and its ped phase.

cards.front: What is the output order of a ped switch pack?
cards.back: Don't Walk, Yellow (normally unused), Walk.

cards.front: What do the flash transfer relays (FTRs) do?
cards.back: In normal operation they connect the switch packs to the field. In flash they drop out and connect the field to the 204 flashers.

cards.front: What do the flash program blocks set?
cards.back: Whether each phase flashes red or yellow when the cabinet is in flash.

cards.front: What flash rate does the CA MUTCD require?
cards.back: 50 to 60 flashes per minute, with the light on for 1/2 to 2/3 of each cycle (4G.01).

cards.front: Does flash come from the controller?
cards.back: No. It comes from the 204 flashers through the FTRs, so the cabinet can flash with the controller removed.

cards.front: How do monitor-caused flash and police-panel flash differ when clearing?
cards.back: Monitor flash latches until someone resets the 210. Police-panel flash clears when the switch goes back to AUTO.

cards.front: What failure is the main reason the 210 monitor exists?
cards.back: A shorted (failed-on) triac that lights a head when the controller says off.

cards.front: How must drivers treat a dark (unpowered) signal in California?
cards.back: As an all-way stop (CVC 21800(d)).

cards.front: What does the 210 conflict monitor do?
cards.back: Watches the field outputs on 16 channels and puts the intersection into flash if two conflicting channels are on together.

cards.front: On the 210 program card, what does a diode in place mean?
cards.back: That pair of channels conflicts. You remove a diode only for a pair allowed to run together.

cards.front: How many diodes are on a 16-channel card, and why?
cards.back: 120: one per pair of channels, 16 × 15 ÷ 2.

cards.front: What are 210 channels 9 to 16 used for?
cards.back: 9 and 10: Overlaps A and B. 11 and 12: special. 13 to 16: Ø2, Ø4, Ø6 and Ø8 peds.

cards.front: When is a ped channel compatible with a vehicle channel?
cards.back: Only if no vehicle on that phase drives or turns through the crosswalk.
cards.note: Ø1 (westbound left) stays in conflict with Ø2P, because it turns through that crosswalk.

cards.front: Besides conflicts, what else trips a 210?
cards.back: Low +24 VDC and a missing controller watchdog signal (CVM).

cards.front: What is the worst mistake you can make on a diode card?
cards.back: Removing a diode for a pair that conflicts. The monitor will then not catch two conflicting greens.

cards.front: What does a Model 2010 monitor add over a 210?
cards.back: Red-fail monitoring, minimum yellow checks and a fault log.

cards.front: Why must a program card never move to another cabinet?
cards.back: Each card matches one intersection's phasing.

cards.front: What does a 12CSC serve, and how many does a pole need?
cards.back: The signal heads on one standard. One 12CSC per pole with heads, as long as the pole needs 12 or fewer conductors.

cards.front: How do you count conductors needed in a 12CSC?
cards.back: 3 per vehicle phase (R, Y, G) + 2 per ped phase (Walk, Don't Walk) + 1 common.

cards.front: What does a 3CSC serve?
cards.back: One push-button location.

cards.front: How many cables does a conduit run carry?
cards.back: One cable for every pole beyond it, because signal cable runs unspliced from the cabinet to each pole. The run leaving the cabinet carries all of them.

cards.front: What is the NEC conduit fill limit for three or more conductors?
cards.back: 40% of the conduit's inside area (NEC Chapter 9, Table 1). 53% for one conductor, 31% for two.

cards.front: How many degrees of bends are allowed between pull points?
cards.back: 360° total (for example NEC 352.26 for PVC).

cards.front: Which conduit runs get an equipment ground or bonding conductor?
cards.back: Every run, including ones that carry only DLC or SIC.

cards.front: How is the equipment grounding conductor sized?
cards.back: By the breaker ahead of the circuit (NEC 250.122): for example 20 A → #12, 30–60 A → #10, 100 A → #8 copper.

cards.front: Why isn't a ground rod by itself enough to protect people?
cards.back: The earth is not an effective fault path (NEC 250.4(A)(5)). The bonding conductor back to the service carries fault current so the breaker trips.

cards.front: What resistance must a single ground rod meet?
cards.back: 25 Ω or less, or a second electrode is added at least 6 ft away (NEC 250.53).

cards.front: What voltage-drop limits does the NEC recommend?
cards.back: 3% on a branch circuit and 5% total (informational note, not a requirement).

cards.front: What color must the grounded (common) conductor be?
cards.back: White or gray (NEC 200.6).

cards.front: What must you do before pulling a switch pack, FTR or monitor?
cards.back: Put the intersection into flash, under traffic control.

cards.front: Why can a cabinet still be live after you open the utility breaker?
cards.back: A battery backup system (BBS) inverter can keep feeding it. Turn the BBS off and verify zero voltage.

cards.front: What should you do before handling wires at a knocked-down pole?
cards.back: Open the signal and lighting breakers at the service and test before touching.

cards.front: Which standard covers arc-flash PPE and verifying a safe work condition?
cards.back: NFPA 70E.

cards.front: Which part of the CA MUTCD covers traffic control for work in the street?
cards.back: Part 6, temporary traffic control.

cards.front: What is the danger of an ungrounded pole or cabinet?
cards.back: A fault can energize it without tripping a breaker, and a person touching it completes the circuit.

cards.front: Why can opening a current-carrying coil be dangerous?
cards.back: Inductive kick: v = L × Δi/Δt. Interrupting 2 A in a 0.4 H coil in 1 ms makes about 800 V.
